analysis.one_liner: Ends billions in federal subsidies, tax breaks, and liability protections for oil, gas, and coal producers.
analysis.headline: Referred to nine House committees on introduction in July 2025; no committee has scheduled it since, and no vote has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would strip away a long list of federal supports for fossil fuel production: more than 20 tax breaks for oil, gas, and coal companies, discounted royalty rates on federal land and offshore waters, limits on how much companies must pay after oil spills, and US-backed financing for fossil fuel projects overseas. It would also repeal parts of recent laws — including provisions of the 2025 'One Big Beautiful Bill Act' — that expanded fossil fuel subsidies, and it would restore an EPA fee on methane leaks from oil and gas operations.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who currently fund tax preferences and discounted royalties for fossil fuel extraction; communities that bear the cost of oil spills, because the bill lifts liability caps and denies tax deductions for spill damages; coal miners and their families, because the bill raises the industry-paid excise tax that funds the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund; and the Treasury, which would collect more from higher royalties and a new 13% tax on offshore Gulf of Mexico production.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers, spill-prone communities, and coal miners

how_it_helps.text: Repeals more than twenty tax preferences for fossil fuel companies, including the enhanced oil recovery credit, percentage depletion for coal, last-in first-out inventory accounting for oil, gas, and coal firms, and the corporate tax exemption for publicly traded partnerships earning fossil fuel income.

Raises the federal royalty rate for coal, oil, and gas extracted from public lands and offshore waters from as low as 12.5% to 18.75%, and ends royalty relief on offshore leases, so the public is paid closer to full value for resources taken from federal land.
Removes statutory limits on what responsible parties owe for offshore oil spills and spills from onshore pipelines carrying tar sands oil, and denies tax deductions for those spill costs.

Prohibits US export and development finance agencies — the Export-Import Bank, the International Development Finance Corporation, USAID, and others — from funding fossil fuel projects, and bars international financial institutions from using US contributions for such projects.
Restores the EPA rule imposing a waste emissions charge on methane leaks from petroleum and natural gas systems by repealing the law that blocked it.
Raises the coal industry-paid excise tax that funds the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund, from $1.10 to $1.38 per ton, shoring up benefits for miners with black lung disease.

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and coal companies, which would lose tax breaks, pay higher royalties, face a new 13% tax on Gulf of Mexico offshore production, and carry unlimited spill liability. Large banks and investment firms with $10 billion or more in assets would lose their exemption from cleanup liability under the Superfund law when they lend to polluting facilities.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil, gas, and coal producers; large banks

drawbacks.text: Removing tax breaks and adding a 13% severance tax on offshore Gulf production would raise producers' costs, and some of that could be passed on to consumers in the form of higher fuel prices, at least at the margin.

The bill terminates the federal carbon capture credit and narrows the clean hydrogen credit to hydrogen made from renewable electricity only, which would eliminate incentives that some climate advocates see as useful tools for cutting emissions from industry.

It repeals recent permitting reforms, including the BUILDER Act changes to the National Environmental Policy Act, which opponents of slower permitting of all kinds — including clean energy infrastructure — argue add delay and cost to construction projects broadly, not just fossil fuel ones.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains go to diffuse beneficiaries — taxpayers, spill-exposed communities, miners — while the costs fall on a concentrated industry that can be expected to pass some costs to consumers. The bill's weakness is breadth: by bundling dozens of subsidy repeals with permitting changes and the termination of carbon capture and hydrogen credits, it invites opponents to attack the most contestable provisions, and its all-or-nothing scope makes partial adoption harder.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went nowhere past its introduction — the Speaker sent it to nine committees, and none has taken it up, so it sits without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

narrative.text: Representative Ilhan Omar introduced the End Polluter Welfare Act of 2025 on July 23, 2025, with 22 Democratic cosponsors.

On the day of introduction, the House referred the bill to nine committees — Ways and Means plus Transportation and Infrastructure, Natural Resources, Science, Energy and Commerce, Agriculture, Appropriations, Financial Services, and Foreign Affairs — with consideration periods to be determined by the Speaker.
No committee has held a hearing or markup, and no floor vote has occurred; the only recorded action since introduction is the referral itself.

The bill would repeal subsidy provisions enacted in recent legislation, including parts of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025 that added fossil fuel tax preferences and directed oil and gas leasing, and it would restore the EPA methane fee rule that Congress disapproved.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, fossil fuel producers: because the bill has not advanced, the existing subsidies, discounted royalties, and liability limits it targets all remain in effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers keep their subsidies

for.name: Rep. Ilhan Omar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to eliminate fossil fuel subsidies and assembled 22 original cosponsors.

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral as chair of the lead committee on the bill's tax provisions; no markup or hearing has been scheduled.

against.name: Speaker of the House
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to nine committees on introduction, splitting it across jurisdictions, and no further action has been scheduled.

against.name: Fossil fuel industry trade associations
against.role: Industry lobby opposing repeal of oil, gas, and coal tax preferences
against.what_they_did: The oil and gas industry has long opposed and lobbied against repeal of production subsidies and royalty increases of this kind.

sides.party_line_note: All 23 supporters are Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-controlled House has taken no action beyond the day-one referral.

industries.note: The bill ends more than twenty tax breaks, raises royalty rates from as low as 12.5% to 18.75%, ends royalty relief, lifts spill liability caps, and adds a 13% tax on Gulf of Mexico offshore production. The public currently absorbs these costs; the bill shifts them back to producers.

The bill repeals percentage depletion for coal, capital gains treatment for coal royalties, and recent coal-specific credits, and raises the black lung excise tax the industry pays to fund miners' benefits.

industries.industry: Large banks and asset managers lending to polluters
industries.note: The bill removes the Superfund law exemption that shields lenders from cleanup liability, targeting banks with $10 billion or more in assets and investment firms with $250 billion or more under management, exposing them to cleanup costs when financed facilities pollute.

The bill terminates the 45Q carbon sequestration credit and narrows the clean hydrogen credit to hydrogen made from renewable electricity, eliminating revenue streams for these industries while ending subsidies that largely supported enhanced oil recovery and fossil-linked hydrogen.

analysis.trajectory: With a Republican-controlled House, no Republican cosponsors, referral to nine committees, and no action since July 2025, the bill is very unlikely to receive a markup or floor vote before this Congress ends; bills at this stage with this support typically die in committee.
